title: Lean Weekly
description: News about Lean, the theorem prover and programming language.

items.title: Pranava Kumar registers a Lean proof of Nivat's conjecture with Palomar
items.content_html:
The entry formalizes Pranava Kumar's manuscript, proving that any configuration on the integer plane over a finite alphabet with at most k times n distinct k by n patterns has a nonzero global period. Its independent Challenge states the full conjecture using only standard Mathlib notions; the 339-file proof needs only Lean's foundational axioms.

Sources: palomar-registry.org, PranavaKCode/nivat-lean

items.title: Ziqing Xiang formalizes Haemers' conjecture for the generalized spectrum in Lean
items.content_html:
The Mathlib-based formalization contains the accompanying paper's whole proof that the proportion of n-vertex graphs determined by their generalized spectrum (the spectra of the adjacency matrices of a graph and its complement) tends to 1 as n grows. It also proves the results the paper quotes from the literature, including Kneser's addition theorem.

Sources: palomar-registry.org, ziqingxiang/dgs

items.title: Haruhisa Enomoto formalizes two classical theorems of Bautista, Gabriel, Roiter and Salmerón
items.content_html:
Built on Mathlib, the complete formalization follows Haruhisa Enomoto's new proof that representation-finite algebras over algebraically closed fields have normed multiplicative bases (closed under products up to zero) and basic ones in characteristic other than two are standard (indecomposable modules match their Auslander–Reiten quiver's mesh category). It also proves the Auslander–Reiten theory it uses.

Sources: palomar-registry.org, haruhisa-enomoto/multiplicative-bases-deformations

items.title: Giulio rebuffo's Janus verifies compiled Go arm64 machine code in Lean 4
items.content_html:
Janus, an early work in progress, decodes instructions in Lean and does not trust the Go compiler, linker, or any source-level reasoning. Every load and store must fall inside a caller-provided allocation, and Go runtime panic stubs (bounds checks, nil, divide) are named outcomes, so "this function never panics" is provable.

Sources: Giulio2002/Janus

items.title: Alexander Meiburg disproves perfect randomized composition for total functions, checked in Lean
items.content_html:
Perfect randomized composition (a composition's randomized query complexity is always at least a constant times the product of its factors' complexities) was known to fail for partial Boolean functions but open for total ones. The main result is machine-checked in Lean 4 as a little-o statement on a subsequence of the construction.

Sources: arXiv:2610.31638, paperswithlean.com

items.title: Tanner Duve of Logical Intelligence offers Veil an invariant-synthesis tactic
items.content_html:
Written for Veil, a Lean-based verifier for transition systems, #synthesize_invariants runs the universal PDR algorithm on a module and its safety property. It returns inductive invariants or a counterexample (both proven sound), a "no universal invariant" result (not proven sound) or "unknown"; it succeeded on every Veil example tested within its supported fragment.

Sources: leanprover.zulipchat.com, verse-lab/veil

items.title: Sebastian Ullrich proposes precomputed prefix trees to speed up Lean imports
items.content_html:
The open pull request replaces hash maps of imported constants, built eagerly at import time, with per-module prefix trees precomputed when oleans are written and merged lazily on first access. The change cuts import Lean wall-clock time by 28% and Mathlib's import phase by 21%, in exchange for about 6% larger standard library oleans.

Sources: lean4#14362

items.title: Leo de Moura publishes MiniForth, a Lean tutorial for programming language semantics
items.content_html:
MiniForth's Forth-inspired teaching language, whose programs act on a stack, has arithmetic, DUP, SWAP, DROP, calls, and conditionals. The tutorial embeds it as Lean functions (a shallow embedding) and as data (a deep embedding), proves program equivalences, and adds a second pass where grind handles routine reasoning; the build checks the examples and proofs.

Sources: leodemoura/MiniForth

items.title: ATOMSLab's LeanSMILES formalizes molecular representations and learning algorithms in Lean
items.content_html:
The repository's SMILES toolkit parses SMILES strings into typed molecular graphs, with a canonicity proof for canonical SMILES and an order-invariance proof for RDKit-compatible Morgan fingerprints. Its LeanLearn library covers linear and logistic regression, and the machine-learning pipeline from SMILES to model runs in Lean, with results checked against scikit-learn.

Sources: ATOMSLab/LeanSMILES

items.title: AI agents help researchers discover a new consensus protocol, verified in Lean
items.content_html:
AI-greement, an agent harness with a Lean-based verification framework, helped researchers discover A-greement, a consensus protocol proved linearizable in about 98,000 lines of Lean. A-greement cuts mean latency over the fastest baseline by 12.2% on write-heavy and 33.3% on read-heavy workloads, and the harness's Lean formalization uncovered four previously unreported vulnerabilities in existing protocols.

Sources: arXiv:2610.30114, paperswithlean.com

items.title: Kraken Lean project proves FFmpeg's SBR decoder binary safe
items.content_html:
The theorem sbr_session_safe covers the linked machine code (aacsbr.o with its callees): given the link's layout, external routines' contracts and a 32-bit bound on their stack, every run stays in the memory it owns and uses at most the stated stack. The prefix-code and bound facts of FFmpeg's Huffman tables are proved.

Sources: zrlk/kraken

items.title: Leo de Moura adds three lia changes that avoid large case splits
items.content_html:
The pull requests, merged October 20 and 21, add dynamic variable reordering before large Cooper splits (case splits with as many cases as a variable's coefficient), exact elimination of equations without unit coefficients, and divisibility normalization. Chains of such equations from / and % definitions no longer yield Cooper splits with thousands of cases.

Sources: lean4#15835, lean4#15838, lean4#15827

items.title: Joris Roos formalizes OpenAI's L³ trilinear Hilbert transform bound with coding agents
items.content_html:
The Lean 4 formalization, about 194,000 lines of code, verifies the main result of a preprint OpenAI made public on October 6, 2026 without an accompanying formalization. The theorem statement is human-written, while Codex and Claude coding agents, following a blueprint generated by GPT-6 Astra Pro, autoformalized the proof over about eight days.

Sources: roos-j/lean-trilinearht, palomar-registry.org

items.title: Carlo Ciliberto, Alessandro Rudi, Enrico Tassi introduce Proof-Carrying Contracts for AI agents
items.content_html:
An execution system called the Airlock runs a tool call only if the Lean kernel accepts the agent's proof that the call preserves the agreed constraints in every case its model allows. A Lean 4 mechanization proves the constraints hold at every instant of execution, even for an adversarial agent, under stated assumptions.

Sources: arXiv:2610.28484, consequential-ai/proof-carrying-contracts, paperswithlean.com

items.title: Matija Bucić, Fankang He and Hyunwoo Lee prove Erdős-Szemerédi sunflower conjecture
items.content_html:
Posed in the 1970s, the conjecture bounds the size of any family of subsets containing no k-sunflower and was previously known only for k = 3, via cap-set results. According to paperswithlean.com, the proof was machine-verified in Lean 4, with the formalization to be released in the Palomar repository.

Sources: arXiv:2610.26686, paperswithlean.com

items.title: Aditya Ranjan Jha and coauthors mechanize a hardware type system in Lean
items.content_html:
Pact, a typed extension of the Anvil hardware description language, checks each component against its type, and compatible types guarantee communication safety (no unsynchronized exchanges or loss of progress). The POPL 2027 paper's artifact includes a Lean 4 mechanization proving soundness of type inference, type checking, and compatibility, plus optimality of inferred types.

Sources: arXiv:2610.26599, doi.org

items.title: Linux 7.3 works around AMD CPU bug behind Lean build segfaults
items.content_html:
The FRO noticed probabilistic segfaults while compiling big Lean projects on certain AMD CPUs running Linux 6.15 or later, and reported them to the Linux kernel. Users of AMD Zen 5 CPUs on kernels 6.15 through 7.2 should consider kernel 7.3 and/or the latest AMD microcode, or, failing that, boot with the option tlbi=ipi.

Sources: leanprover.zulipchat.com, lore.kernel.org

items.title: Ilya Sergey describes Vermilion, an experimental Lean backend for Rust verifier Verus
items.content_html:
Vermilion expresses Verus's verification conditions (mathematical propositions about a program), normally sent to the Z3 solver, as Lean theorems, though it does not prove that they correctly describe Rust's semantics. Its default tactic, vrml, tries to prove each automatically, and any it leaves open can be proved interactively, drawing on Mathlib.

Sources: proofsandintuitions.net, @ilyasergey on X

items.title: Anirudh Gupta, Siddhartha Gadgil and Petros Markopoulos present PastaLean for verifying Python
items.content_html:
PastaLean deterministically translates Python into Lean through Python's abstract syntax tree, with no LLM, turning specifications written in Python into theorems for agents or humans to prove. It also includes TypeInfer, a Python type inference engine that completed one benchmark in 1.25 s against HeaderGen's 36.2 s, and an MCP server for coding agents.

Sources: anirudhg07.github.io, siddhartha-gadgil/PastaLean, leanprover.zulipchat.com

items.title: Jeremy Avigad and coauthors back formalizing all of mathematics, if done well
items.content_html:
The Xena guest post, co-written by Kevin Buzzard, Johan Commelin, Rémy Degenne, Kim Morrison, Oliver Nash and Adam Topaz, follows a big OpenAI release and warns against building formal libraries nobody uses. It highlights Tau Ceti, an AI-written library slightly larger than Mathlib, and says most of mathematics can be formalized within three years.

Sources: xenaproject.wordpress.com

items.title: Shanghai AI Lab's Shusheng-S2 helps prove 3D Ghys conjecture, verified in Lean
items.content_html:
Tech Times calls Shusheng-S2 the first Chinese AI model to help resolve a world-class open conjecture in pure mathematics: the three-dimensional Ghys conjecture, unresolved for 31 years. A Peking University team, using up to 100 AI agents, independently verified every logical step of Jiesong Zhang's proof, producing more than 550,000 lines of Lean code.

Sources: techtimes.com, pandaily.com

items.title: Anthropic's Claude designs more efficient quantum circuits, verifying one with Lean proofs
items.content_html:
Working largely on its own, Claude Mythos 5 produced circuits that improve on the best published versions. For a new circuit computing modular inversion, the wraparound version of division, Claude checked the formula behind the design with large-scale numerical simulations, then formalized the claim in Lean, a step Anthropic attributes to the model's caution.

Sources: anthropic.com, arXiv:2610.22367

items.title: SAIR launches Open Math OS, a research workspace built on open models
items.content_html:
Open Math OS offers open-source models and AI agents that explore problems in parallel, and gives every project a 24/7 cloud machine with more than 100 mathematical and scientific computing tools preinstalled. Compute is free for approved teams, the mathematical community owns its data, and launch partners include Hugging Face, Lean, CSCS and EPFL.

Sources: openmathmodel.org, @SAIRfoundation on X

items.title: Vasily Ilin shares a prompt to build verified, faster software in Lean
items.content_html:
The prompt asks for a Lean version of software X, proved correct and optimized to run at least 10% faster than X's fastest implementation, with tests and proofs passing throughout. Kim Morrison's lean-zip, a verified DEFLATE implementation, inspired the workflow; examples cover integer factorization and jump processes, the latter faster than Julia's JumpProcesses.jl.

Sources: @IlinVasily29521 on X, Vilin97/PrimeFactorLean, Vilin97/JumpProcessesLean, kim-em/lean-zip

items.title: Lean now ships verified kernels (proof checkers) and a lake check command
items.content_html:
Leo de Moura writes that AI agents are effective at finding vulnerabilities in Lean's kernel. Lean v4.35.0's lake check rechecks a project with leanchecker, the official Lean kernel without the baggage around it, and lake check --paranoid runs four additional kernels, including con-leche, the first kernel for Lean written in Lean and proven consistent.

Sources: leodemoura.github.io

items.title: OpenAI publishes 719 model-produced math manuscripts, about 42% Lean-formalized
items.content_html:
OpenAI's openai/math repository holds manuscripts and proof artifacts produced by an internal OpenAI model, organized into 372 families, with 300 of 719 top-line results formalized in Lean. An October 7, 2026 update withdrew three manuscripts after a sign error and revised 14 others.

Sources: openai/math

items.title: Machine-checked Lean 4 proof of the general Courtade–Kumar inequality released
items.content_html:
A repository by @dpwoodru contains a complete, machine-checked Lean 4 proof of the general Courtade–Kumar inequality (the most informative Boolean function conjecture), formalizing the paper by Z. Chen, A. Gohari, A. Javanmard, H. Lin, V. Mirrokni, C. Nair and D. P. Woodruff. The whole proof spans 45,500 modules.

Sources: dpwoodru/general-courtade-kumar-lean

items.title: Emina Torlak presents SymCert, a Lean framework for verified Cedar policy analyses
items.content_html:
SymCert, implemented in Lean, builds verified SMT-based analyses of Cedar policies, an open-source authorization language. In the FMCAD 2026 paper, five analyses used in a Cedar analysis service at Amazon Web Services were modeled and proved in one work day, and three extensions for new Cedar features took 4 to 8 days each.

Sources: paper (pdf)

items.title: AxiomProver generates Lean proof of Collatz positive density results
items.content_html:
CollatzPosDens, a Palomar registry entry, formally proves the main results of Kenny Lau's paper "Explicit positive lower density for the Collatz Conjecture", including Theorem 1.3, an explicit positive density of odd starting values reaching a prescribed target not divisible by 3. AxiomProver, Axiom Math's in-house theorem proving system, generated the Lean files.

Sources: palomar-registry.org, AxiomMath/CollatzPositiveDensity

items.title: Flapjack ports the verified Pancake compiler from HOL4 to Lean
items.content_html:
Flapjack is bringing the Pancake compiler, originally verified in HOL4, and its proofs to Lean, with a path compiling a fragment of Pancake to RISC-V where all stages except parsing and AST conversion have a correctness theorem. A MIPS32 backend targets the Ziren zkVM, but its output has been run only on Ziren's Lean model.

Sources: flapjack-lang.dev

items.title: Joachim Breitner and Lean FRO describe the proof behind con-leche checker
items.content_html:
con-leche, a checker for Lean 4, comes with a proof in Lean that every environment it accepts has a model in set theory, so no accepted environment holds a proof of False. A new document gives a pen-and-paper account of that argument on a simplified fragment of the checker.

Sources: leanprover.github.io

items.title: Lean 4 merges libuv buffer fix and refactor from Sofia Rodrigues
items.content_html:
The fix, merged October 14, makes send and recv fail with an invalid-argument error for buffers of 4 GiB or more, instead of letting the length wrap to 32 bits. The refactor, merged October 15, adds owned_ref, a helper that owns Lean objects and helps avoid hundreds of lean_inc and lean_dec in libuv code.

Sources: lean4#15598, lean4#15603

items.title: Thomas Browning and coauthors release AnnalsChallenge, 50 Annals theorems stated in Lean
items.content_html:
Each statement, written by hand in Lean 4 using Mathlib, is the main result of an Annals of Mathematics paper published since 2020; all were manually reviewed, then audited by AI, and are released without formalized proofs. The authors say measuring progress in AI autoformalization of mathematics requires hard, trustworthy datasets of formal statements.

Sources: arXiv:2610.18301

items.title: Google's Gemini 4 Argon writes a Lean-verified quantum arcsin implementation
items.content_html:
Google's launch post for Gemini 4 Argon (dated 2026-10-13) reports an arcsin implementation, a building block in recent quantum simulation algorithms, written by Argon and formally verified in Lean. It cuts spacetime cost by more than 100x compared to a published quantum CORDIC baseline.

Sources: blog.google

items.title: Julia Markus Himmel reworks order instances across Lean core types
items.content_html:
Julia Markus Himmel redefined the order on String as the lexicographic order of its UTF-8 encoding, made Min Float follow the IEEE-754-2019 minimum operation, and added missing order instances for BitVec, List, Array, Vector and ByteArray. Sofia Rodrigues fixed leaks and refactored the libuv bindings.

Sources: lean4#15581, lean4#15257, lean4#15274, lean4#15304, lean4#15329, lean4#15175, lean4#15545

items.title: Lean 4.35.0 ships vcgen, lake check, and bundled independent kernels
items.content_html:
Lean 4.35.0, published on 2026-10-12, adds vcgen, a faster and more general successor of mvcgen, plus lake check and lake comparator, which check a project with Lean's kernel and optionally several independent kernels now included in the toolchain.

Sources: v4.35.0 release notes, lean4 v4.35.0

items.title: Sebastian Ullrich removes Lean's 255-object-field limit per constructor
items.content_html:
A merged pull request by Sebastian Ullrich removes the limit of 255 object fields per constructor, and thus per structure. When a constructor has more, the compiler keeps the first 254 in the constructor object and stores the rest in a chain of spill objects, with one pointer followed per spill object on access.

Sources: lean4#15516

items.title: Sebastian Ullrich merges two fixes to how Lean modules export theorems
items.content_html:
In Lean, an asynchronously elaborated theorem's exported info in a module is now available as soon as its signature is, instead of after its proof is elaborated. A second change stops modules from exporting constants such as foo.eq_1 realized only inside a proof, so such proofs no longer trigger downstream rebuilds.

Sources: lean4#15559, lean4#15563

items.title: AI proof-search agent resolves nine open Erdős problems, verified in Lean
items.content_html:
A paper in Science by George Tsoukalas, Swarat Chaudhuri and coauthors describes an agent for formal proof search that autonomously resolved nine of 353 open Erdős problems and proved 44 of 492 On-Line Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences conjectures. A basic agent alternating LLM-based generation with Lean-based verification replicated the Erdős successes.

Sources: science.org

items.title: Lean reference manual documents vcgen, the successor of mvcgen in Lean 4.35
items.content_html:
A pull request by Sebastian Graf documents the vcgen tactic and its Std.WP framework, adds the tutorial "Verifying Imperative Programs Using vcgen", and moves the mvcgen chapter and tutorial to their own files. The Kraken project already uses vcgen to prove that FFmpeg's FMA3 dot-product loop, over two arrays that may alias, terminates without faulting.

Sources: reference-manual#927, zrlk/kraken

items.title: Renaissance Philanthropy and XTX Markets announce $17.1 million in AI for Math grants
items.content_html:
The AI for Math Fund selected 22 applications representing 30 organizations from more than 470 submissions, bringing its total commitments to $35.1 million. Winners include TorchLean, a Lean-native framework for verified machine learning, and a project turning a Lean 4 visual proofwriting prototype into open-source infrastructure for reading AI-generated proofs.

Sources: renaissancephilanthropy.org

items.title: Scott Armstrong publishes skill files for LLM-driven Lean autoformalization
items.content_html:
Scott Armstrong writes that autoformalization of research-level mathematics has become easy, citing a Lean formalization of a 145-page paper with Vicol in about 36 hours (270k lines of code), and makes the agent skill files public. A separate Xena post weighs mathematicians' reactions to AI, noting "You cannot fool Lean."

Sources: scottnarmstrong.com, xenaproject.wordpress.com

items.title: Sebastian Ullrich makes Lean's type class resolution cache persist across commands
items.content_html:
Two merged pull requests by Sebastian Ullrich keep type class resolution results for later commands and let queries differing only in free variables share a cache entry. Building Mathlib takes about 4% fewer instructions and 8% less wall-clock time, and spends about 16% less time in type class resolution.

Sources: lean4#14369, lean4#14316

items.title: Leo de Moura adds option to run grind on Sym.simp normalizer
items.content_html:
A merged Lean pull request adds backward.grind.normalizer, which switches grind to the Sym.simp-based normalizer when set to false (the default behavior is unchanged). Related changes add grind_norm, a debugging tactic whose check mode runs both normalizers and fails when results differ, and fix negation-pushing rewrites that had been dead code since #9271.

Sources: lean4#15464, lean4#15375, lean4#15378

items.title: Lean core gains an HTML type, renderer, and HTML-like syntax
items.content_html:
Wojciech Nawrocki merged pull requests adding Lean.Data.Html, a type of HTML forests aimed at authoring HTML, with a renderer to String, plus HTML-like syntax and an elaborator into that type. Separately, Emilio Jesús Gallego Arias added optional VIR support and a small Lean-to-JavaScript client example on Lean 4.35 to Verso Blueprint.

Sources: lean4#14935, lean4#15002, verso-blueprint#491

items.title: Four authors formalize the Hamilton-Perelman proof of the Poincaré conjecture in Lean
items.content_html:
Ziyang Qin, Yuan Liao, Ayush Khaitan, and Bennett Chow formalize the smooth three-dimensional Poincaré conjecture via Ricci flow with surgery and finite-time extinction. Together with the Moise smoothing theorem, the result yields the topological three-dimensional Poincaré conjecture.

Sources: arXiv:2609.33842

items.title: NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory formalizes a metrology quantity calculus in Lean 4
items.content_html:
NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory's PropertyKindCalculus formalizes René Dybkær's ontology on property, extended with Flater's tracking of kinds of quantities, and is described as the first in which the quantity calculus itself, beyond the taxonomy around it, is a checked artifact. It includes catalogues for eleven of the thirteen ISO/IEC 80000 parts.

Sources: nasa-jpl/PropertyKindCalculus

items.title: lazylean, a lazy-evaluation Lean kernel, competes in the Lean Kernel Arena
items.content_html:
lazylean, a C++ type checker for Lean 4, hands computing terms to a Krivine machine with call-by-need thunks, after Coq's cClosure. The Lean Kernel Arena, which tests and benchmarks proof checkers for Lean, lists lazylean 0.3.0 alongside checkers such as tenet 0.11.1, lean4cobol and nanoclo-fortran.

Sources: corun1024/lazylean, arena.lean-lang.org

items.title: Keith Adler releases Lean Studio, a native desktop IDE for Lean 4
items.content_html:
Lean Studio runs on macOS, Windows and Linux and re-checks every declaration from the compiled .olean files with Tenet, a separate implementation of Lean's type checker. Keith Adler's IDE also includes Prove It, which tries 17 tactics on any sorry at once, and an MCP server for AI assistants.

Sources: keithadler/leanstudio

items.title: Leo de Moura adds a polynomial arithmetic normalizer to Lean's Sym.simp
items.content_html:
A series of merged Lean pull requests adds Sym.Arith.normalize?, which rewrites ring and semiring terms into polynomial normal form with a proof by reflection, and an arith simproc for Sym.simp that uses it. Later changes extend it to relations, ring characteristic, non-commutative rings, and some field rewrites, and grind's ring solver now shares Sym.Arith code.

Sources: lean4#15292, lean4#15279, lean4#15293, lean4#15295, lean4#15297, lean4#15298, lean4#15190
